questions.q: A dependency is listed as "^0.4.2". Which versions can npm install?
questions.explain: Below 1.0.0 every release may break, so a caret only allows changes to the right of the first non-zero number: ^0.4.2 means >=0.4.2 <0.5.0.

questions.q: This translates caret ranges into comparisons, following the 0.x rule. What does it print?
questions.explain: The caret allows changes only to the right of the first non-zero number. For ^0.0.7 that leaves nothing: exactly 0.0.7. For ^0.12.0 only patch versions of 0.12.

questions.q: Your package.json says "^2.3.0". The registry has 2.3.4, 2.4.0-beta.1 and 3.0.0-rc.1. Which does npm install?
questions.explain: Ranges skip prereleases unless the range itself names a prerelease of the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. So only final releases count, and the highest match is 2.3.4.
options: It fails, because a newer prerelease exists

questions.q: Which versions does ^1.3.0-beta.1 allow from this list: 1.3.0-beta.0, 1.3.0-beta.2, 1.3.0, 1.4.0-beta.1, 1.9.0?
questions.explain: Opting into 1.3.0-beta.1 allows later prereleases of 1.3.0 and every normal release up to 2.0.0. Prereleases of other versions, like 1.4.0-beta.1, stay excluded, and beta.0 is lower than the range's start.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Strings compare character by character: "1" is less than "9", so "1.10.0" sorts first and is "smaller". Versions must be compared as numbers, part by part.

questions.q: This compares only prerelease labels, split at the dots. What does it print?
questions.explain: Numeric parts compare as numbers (2 before 10), text parts alphabetically (alpha, beta, rc), and when all shared parts are equal the shorter label comes first (alpha before alpha.1). These are the semver rules.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A prerelease comes before its release, so 2.0.0 is the highest. Build metadata after + is ignored when comparing, so 2.0.0+build.7 equals 2.0.0. (Comparing the cores as strings is only safe here because they are equal; real code compares numbers.)

questions.q: A plugin declares "peerDependencies": { "eslint": "^8.40.0 || ^9.0.0" }. Which ESLint version does it not accept?
questions.explain: || means either range. 8.30.0 is a version 8, but below 8.40.0, so it fails the first range and is not a 9.

questions.q: Your project depends on debug@2, and five of Express's packages depend on debug@4. Where does npm put them?
questions.explain: Your direct dependency gets the top-level slot. Packages that need an incompatible version get their own copy in their own node_modules, which is how the lesson's install ended up with six copies of debug.
options: debug@2 in node_modules/debug, and a nested copy of debug@4 inside each package that needs it
One debug@4 for everyone, because it is newer
debug@4 at the top and debug@2 nested inside your project folder
npm refuses to install two major versions

questions.q: In npm ls, what does ms@2.1.3 deduped mean?
questions.explain: Node.js looks for packages in the nearest node_modules and then in parent folders. One hoisted copy can serve every package whose range it satisfies.
options: This package's need for ms is met by a copy installed higher in the tree

questions.q: A deep dependency, three levels down, has a security fix in a new patch version, but its parent pins the old version exactly. What lets you use the fix today?
questions.explain: overrides forces a version anywhere in the tree. You are now promising compatibility on the parent's behalf, so test it, and remove the override when the parent updates. Edits inside node_modules vanish on the next install.
options: An overrides entry in your package.json, followed by testing
Nothing, you must wait for the parent to update

questions.q: Two copies of the same validation library are installed. Each copy defines its own class, simulated here by two identical class definitions. What does this print?
questions.explain: Same name, same code, different class objects. instanceof checks identity, so an error from one copy is not an instance of the other copy's class. This is a real bug caused by duplicated packages.

questions.q: This reads part of a lockfile's packages object. What does it print?
questions.explain: The key "" is your own project. Packages flagged dev are only reachable through dev dependencies, so a production install (npm ci --omit=dev) installs only lodash.

questions.q: What does the integrity field in package-lock.json protect against?
questions.explain: It is a SHA-512 hash of the tarball. npm refuses any download that does not match. It fixes the exact bytes of the version you locked; it cannot judge whether that version is safe.
options: Installing a tarball whose bytes differ from the ones recorded, for example a replaced or corrupted download
A maintainer publishing a malicious new version

questions.q: Why should a CI build run npm ci rather than npm install?
questions.explain: npm ci gives every build the same tree you tested. Skipping dev dependencies needs --omit=dev, which a test build usually does not want.
options: It installs exactly what the lockfile says, never rewrites it, and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree
It is the only command that runs tests
It installs the newest versions allowed by the ranges

questions.q: Two branches both added dependencies, and package-lock.json has a merge conflict. What should you do?
questions.explain: The lockfile is generated. npm rebuilds a correct one from the merged package.json. Hand-edited lockfiles are easy to get subtly wrong, with integrity hashes that do not match.
options: Resolve package.json, take either version of the lockfile, then run npm install to regenerate it
Edit the conflict markers in the lockfile by hand
Delete the lockfile and never commit it again

questions.q: npm install fails with ERESOLVE ... peer react@"^19.3.0" from react-dom@19.3.0 ... Found: react@18.3.1. What is the right fix?
questions.explain: The authors of react-dom 19 say it needs React 19. Forcing the install gives you a combination known not to work, and it will fail at run time instead.
options: Make the versions agree: install React 19 with react-dom 19, or use react-dom 18
Install react-dom as a dev dependency

questions.q: Why does react-dom declare React as a peer dependency instead of a normal dependency?
questions.explain: A plugin needs the host package the project installed. A peer dependency says "my user provides this, in a version I accept", so there is exactly one copy.
options: It must use the same React copy as the rest of the app; as a normal dependency it could get its own copy
So that React is only installed in development

questions.q: How do you pass --watch to the command behind "test": "node --test"?
questions.explain: Arguments after -- are appended to the script's command. Without --, npm reads --watch as an option for itself.
options: npm run test:watch always, there is no other way

questions.q: A package has scripts prebuild, build and postbuild. You run npm run build and prebuild exits with code 1. What happens?
questions.explain: npm runs the three in order and stops at the first failure, passing its exit code on, which is what a CI job needs.
options: build and postbuild do not run, and npm run build exits with 1

questions.q: This script is run as npm run build in a package named invoice-kit, version 1.2.0. npm set the environment variables shown in the first line. What does it print?
questions.explain: npm hands scripts information through environment variables, and environment variables are always strings. npm_lifecycle_event is the script name, without "npm run".

questions.q: A script "clean": "rm -rf dist" fails for a teammate on Windows. What is the most robust fix?
questions.explain: npm runs scripts in sh on macOS and Linux but in cmd.exe on Windows, which has no rm -rf. Node.js runs the same everywhere.
options: Replace it with a small Node.js script, node scripts/clean.js, that uses fs.rm
Tell the teammate to stop using Windows

questions.q: Which script is the right place for "run the tests before every publish"?
questions.explain: prepublishOnly runs only before npm publish. Install scripts would run on every user's machine, which is both wasteful and exactly what attackers abuse.

questions.q: Why test a package by installing the npm pack tarball instead of through a workspace link?
questions.explain: A link exposes the whole folder, so files excluded by files still work locally and hide the mistake. The tarball is exactly what your users will receive.
options: The tarball contains only what would really be published, so a missing file or wrong exports path shows up

questions.q: A package's package.json has "exports": "./index.js". A user writes import { helper } from "invoice-kit/internal.js". What happens?
questions.explain: exports defines the public surface. Everything else is private, so the author can reorganise internal files without breaking users.
options: The import fails, because only the entry points listed in exports can be imported
It works, every file in the package can be imported
npm refuses to install the package

questions.q: npm publish --dry-run for @naija-shop/invoice-kit says "default access". What must you add on the first real publish to make it public?
questions.explain: Scoped packages default to restricted (private) access, which requires a paid account. Public scoped packages need the access flag once.
options: Nothing, scoped packages are public by default

questions.q: You publish 2.0.0-beta.1 of a popular package. What should happen to the latest tag?
questions.explain: npm install your-package installs whatever latest points at. npm 11 refuses to publish a prerelease without an explicit --tag for this reason.
options: It must stay on the last stable version; publish the beta with --tag next
It should move to the beta so people test it
It does not matter, ranges ignore dist-tags

questions.q: Your package is at 1.1.0. Which command makes 1.2.0-beta.0?
questions.explain: prerelease from a release makes a prerelease of the next patch (1.1.1-beta.0). preminor and premajor make prereleases of the next minor and major.

questions.q: You published 1.4.0 with a wrong VAT rate a week ago. What do you do?
questions.explain: Published versions are immutable, and unpublishing is heavily restricted (for example, within 72 hours and only when nothing depends on the version). A new patch plus a deprecation warning is the normal fix.
options: Publish 1.4.1 with the fix and npm deprecate 1.4.0 with a message
Edit the published tarball on the registry
Delete the package and publish it under a new name

questions.q: What does publishing with provenance give your users?
questions.explain: Provenance links a package to its source and build, so users can check it was not built on some attacker's laptop. It says nothing about whether the code itself is good.
options: A signed statement of which source repository and which CI workflow built the package
A guarantee that the package has no vulnerabilities

questions.q: Your company has a private package called shop-auth on an internal registry. What is the dependency-confusion risk?
questions.explain: Unscoped private names can be claimed publicly by anyone. Use a scope you own (@naija-shop/auth) and point that scope at your registry in .npmrc.
options: An attacker publishes a public shop-auth with a higher version, and a misconfigured install fetches it from the public registry
The internal registry leaks the package to the public
Two developers cannot install it at the same time

questions.q: npm audit reports a high-severity ReDoS in a package used only by your test runner, and nothing with --omit=dev. What is the sensible response?
questions.explain: Severity describes the bug, not your exposure. A ReDoS needs attacker-controlled input to the vulnerable function, and a test tool reading your own files does not get that. Still update it, just not in a panic.
options: Update it when convenient; it does not run in production, so it is not an emergency
Stop the release until it is fixed

questions.q: npm suggests npm audit fix --force. What does --force allow that plain npm audit fix does not?
questions.explain: Without --force, fixes stay inside your ranges. With it, npm may jump majors. Update such packages deliberately and read their changelogs, or use an override for transitive ones.
options: Updating a package past its range, including to a new major version that may break your code
Nothing, it just skips the confirmation

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "crossenv" needs one inserted hyphen. "lodahs" needs two replacements (h→s and s→h), because edit distance counts a swap of neighbours as two edits. Identical names have distance 0.

questions.q: A library pins its dependency exactly, "ms": "2.1.2", and another library in the same app pins "ms": "2.1.3". What is the effect?
questions.explain: Exact pins in libraries prevent sharing. Libraries should use ^ ranges so npm can deduplicate; applications get their exact versions from the lockfile.
options: The app gets two copies of ms, because no single version satisfies both
The app gets no copy of ms

questions.q: npm picks the highest matching version, unless the latest tag also matches. What does this simplified resolver print?
questions.explain: 5.3.0 is higher, but the publisher has not moved latest to it, so a range that latest satisfies resolves to latest. For ^4.0.0 the highest 4.x wins. No 6.x exists, so npm would report ETARGET.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: This is exactly ^0.2.3: at least 0.2.3 and below 0.3.0. It matches the npx semver --range "^0.2.3" output in the lesson.

questions.q: npm marks a package dev when it is reachable only through dev dependencies. What does this print?
questions.explain: Everything reachable only through vitest is dev-only, including its own dependencies. If lodash also depended on picocolors, picocolors would be needed in production and lose its dev flag.

questions.q: Write compare(a, b) for plain versions MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (no prereleases). Return a negative number if a is lower, positive if higher, 0 if equal. The program sorts a list with it.
questions.explain: Convert each part to a number and compare left to right; the first difference decides. Comparing the strings directly would put 1.10.0 before 1.9.3.

questions.q: Extend version comparison to prereleases: compare(a, b) first compares MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; if equal, a version without a prerelease label is higher; if both have labels, compare the labels as plain strings (enough for this test).
questions.explain: A prerelease comes before its release, but after every lower release: 2.0.1-alpha.1 is still above 2.0.0, because the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH part is compared first. Real semver also compares numeric label parts as numbers.

questions.q: Write tildeRange(range) that turns ~X.Y.Z into the pair of comparisons it means: >=X.Y.Z <X.(Y+1).0.
questions.explain: A tilde allows patch updates only. Note that ~0.9.0 goes up to 0.10.0, not 1.0.0: 9 + 1 is 10, and versions are numbers, not digits.

questions.q: Write satisfies(version, range) for ranges made of comparisons joined by spaces (AND) and || (OR), such as ">=1.2.0 <1.5.0 || >=2.1.0". Support >=, < and <=. A cmp helper is given.
questions.explain: OR sets are checked with some, and the comparisons inside a set with every. This matches what npx semver --range printed for the same list in the lesson.

questions.q: Write whoNeeds(packages, name): given a lockfile's packages object, return the names of the packages (or "(root)" for the key "") whose dependencies include name. This is the heart of npm explain.
questions.explain: A reverse lookup over the lockfile answers "why is this installed?". Taking the text after the last node_modules/ also works for nested and scoped packages.

questions.q: Write parseIntegrity(value) for lockfile integrity strings like sha512-3oSe…==. Return { algorithm, bytes }, where bytes is the length of the base64 digest after decoding. Use atob, which decodes base64 to a string of one character per byte.
questions.explain: SHA-512 produces 512 bits, which is 64 bytes. Splitting at the first dash only matters because base64 itself never contains a dash, but it is the safe habit.

questions.q: Write looksLike(name, popular): return the popular names that differ from name by exactly one inserted, deleted or replaced character (and not the name itself). Checking only distance 1 keeps it simple.
questions.explain: Walk both names together and allow one mismatch, skipping a character in the longer name when lengths differ. "axois" swaps two letters, which is two edits, so a distance-1 check misses it: real tools use distance 2 or treat a swap as one edit.

questions.q: Write runOrder(scripts, name) that returns the scripts npm run name would run, in order: pre<name> if it exists, name, then post<name> if it exists. Throw Error("Missing script: NAME") when name itself does not exist.
questions.explain: The hooks are found by name alone. Note the trap in pretest: it runs npm run build, which has its own pre and post hooks, so one npm test runs five scripts. Hooks are convenient, but explicit chains like "test": "npm run build && node --test" are easier to follow.
